replace: statement

A heritability, where one is given, describes how much of the differences between people in one population at one time go with differences in their genes; it is not the share of any one person's risk that comes from genes (the editors' explanation; Visscher et al., 2008, on what heritability means, is not yet read).

A heritability, where one is given, is a ratio: the share of the differences between people in one population, for a trait measured at a particular time or age, that goes with differences in their genes. It is not the share of any one person's risk, or of a trait, that comes from genes; a high heritability does not mean that genes fix the outcome or that the environment cannot change it (human height has a heritability of about 0.8, yet average height has risen over generations); and it says nothing about why groups differ or why levels change over time. Because it depends on how much the genes and the environments vary, it can change when environments change, with age and with how the trait is measured, and in theory a figure from one population does not predict another, though the heritabilities of similar traits are often similar across populations; for a diagnosis, the figure is much smaller on the observed yes-or-no scale than on an assumed underlying scale of liability when the condition is rare; and the classical twin design estimates only three variance components and overstates heritability when identical twins share more of their environment than non-identical twins do, or when genes and environments are correlated (Visscher et al., 2008, a conceptual review by geneticists that discusses no drug-use figure).
plain
A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes.

A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes, it does not mean that the environment cannot change things, and it can change when living conditions change.

The statement that a heritability is not the share of one person's risk is the editors' explanation; the paper the round lists on this point (Visscher et al., 2008) is not yet read.

What a heritability does and does not mean now rests on Visscher et al. (2008), a conceptual narrative review by quantitative geneticists, used for definitions only: it discusses no drug-use figure, its numerical examples (height, IQ, livestock, schizophrenia and depression) are second-hand illustrations, two of its worked examples do not match its own formulas (card reporting issues), and it does not change the rating.

replace: statement
Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read.

Words for the person were tested in one earlier, smaller experiment: of 728 people at talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008 (location not stated), 516 (mean age 51; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree) completed one of two versions of a story about a man in court-ordered treatment who had positive drug and breath tests; those whose version called him 'a substance abuser' agreed slightly more with statements about blame, punishment and non-medical responses than those whose version said he had 'a substance use disorder' (2.92 against 2.82 on a 1–6 scale; d about 0.2), and did not differ detectably in willingness to have him as an employee, neighbour, co-worker or friend, or in treatment-related statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). That study calls itself randomized, but the two versions were handed out alternately; 29% of those handed a form did not complete it; its printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test (two-sided about .04, above the authors' own threshold of .025); and it could not rule out differences of about the same size in social contact or treatment statements.
